## C1 · Attention

L1. **DIRECTOR** · Explain attention. Twenty seconds. ▶ S02 (start): «How an LLM picks its next word»
   _Visual: Dark math look, glowing vector strokes. The prompt types in a corner; the sentence 'The cat sat on the mat because it was tired' writes in as tokens._

L2. **NARRATOR** · A language model turns each word into a point in space, where related meanings sit close together.
   _Visual: On 'space' the tokens lift into a slowly rotating 3D embedding cloud; 'cat' and 'mat' drift near each other. All code original._

L3. **NARRATOR** · Each word looks back and weighs the words before. Here, "it" reaches for "the cat".
   _Visual: Faint attention lines from the last token to every earlier token; on the quoted 'it' the line from 'it' to 'the cat' brightens. Small corner tag: ILLUSTRATIVE._

L4. **NARRATOR** · Then it gives every word it knows a probability, and bets on one. ▶ S02 (end): «How an LLM picks its next word»
   _Visual: Probability bars race for the next-word slot; on 'bets' one bar is sampled and drops into the sentence as the next token. Pull-back to the film strip._


## C2 · Completing the square

L1. **DIRECTOR** · Baghdad, ninth century. Complete the square. ▶ S03 (start): «The 1,200-year-old trick behind the quadratic formula»
   _Visual: Watercolor wash: a Baghdad courtyard, a master and a student at a table. The prompt types over the wash in ink._

L2. **STUDENT** · A square and ten roots make thirty-nine. I am stuck.
   _Visual: Clean ink over the wash: an x-by-x square, then on 'ten' a 10-wide-by-x rectangle beside it; the label '= 39' (no symbols spoken). Student character is dramatized._

L3. **KHWARIZMI** · Split the ten in half. Five on two sides.
   _Visual: On 'half' the rectangle splits; two 5-wide strips swing onto two sides of the square._

L4. **KHWARIZMI** · Now a corner is missing: five by five.
   _Visual: On 'corner' the empty 5x5 gap glows amber; '25' writes inside it._

L5. **KHWARIZMI** · Fill it, and the square is whole: eight by eight. The root is three.
   _Visual: On 'fill' the corner fills and the perfect 8x8 square locks (insight sting); 39 + 25 = 64 writes beside it; the side reads 5 + 3, and the 3 glows._

L6. **NARRATOR** · That was al-Khwarizmi, and his al-jabr gave algebra its name.
   _Visual: The master's name inks in beneath the figure; on 'al-jabr' the word unfolds into 'algebra'._

L7. **NARRATOR** · He wrote it all in words. Centuries later, the picture became a formula. ▶ S03 (end): «The 1,200-year-old trick behind the quadratic formula»
   _Visual: A 'centuries later' caption first; only then does the figure morph into symbols, and on 'formula' the quadratic formula assembles. Pull-back to the film strip._


## C3 · P versus NP

L1. **DIRECTOR** · P versus NP. Make it hurt. ▶ S04 (start): «Checking is easy. Is finding easy?»
   _Visual: Dark math look. The prompt types; the background dims a step on 'hurt'._

L2. **NARRATOR** · Checking a finished puzzle takes a second. Finding the answer may not.
   _Visual: A filled sudoku grid ticks green row by row within one second; beside it a search tree starts branching. No 'NP-complete' caption._

L3. **NARRATOR** · As the puzzle grows, the search explodes.
   _Visual: The grid grows larger; a plot race of n squared, n cubed and 2 to the n; on 'explodes' the 2^n curve goes vertical and the tree fills the frame._

L4. **NARRATOR** · P equals NP would mean anything checkable in polynomial time is also solvable in polynomial time.
   _Visual: On-screen definition in LaTeX, 'polynomial time' on both sides; on 'solvable' the two halves of the definition link with an equals sign and a question mark._

L5. **NARRATOR** · Nobody knows. A proof is worth a million dollars.
   _Visual: On 'million' a card: '$1,000,000 Millennium Prize'._

L6. **NARRATOR** · AI might help find that proof. On other problems, it has already found new mathematics. ▶ S04 (end): «Checking is easy. Is finding easy?»
   _Visual: Two small cards on 'mathematics': 'FunSearch: new cap-set constructions (2023)' and 'AlphaEvolve: improved algorithms (2025)', each stamped 'not P vs NP'. Pull-back to the film strip._


## C4 · Kepler's page

L1. **DIRECTOR** · Kepler. Show me the actual page.  `[Harmonices Mundi (Linz, 1619), Book V ch. III, p. 189]` ▶ S05 (start): «Kepler's sentence that ran the solar system»
   _Visual: Engraved-plate style. On 'page' the real 1619 scan slides in (public-domain scan; rights of the archive.org scan still to confirm)._

L2. **NARRATOR** · In 1619, Kepler wrote a sentence he called most certain and most exact.  `[Harmonices Mundi p. 189]`
   _Visual: On 'sentence' an amber highlight sweeps the Latin 'Sed res est certissima exactissimaque ...'; a translation panel slides in._

L3. **NARRATOR** · A planet's period grows with its distance to the power of one and a half.
   _Visual: Translation panel: 'the ratio of the periods is precisely the 3/2 power of the ratio of the mean distances'. Optional (first cut if tight): the equal-areas wedge sweeps, labeled '2nd law, 1609'._

L4. **NARRATOR** · Plot the six planets he knew, and they fall on one straight line. His word for it: exactly.  `[NASA NSSDCA Planetary Fact Sheet]` ▶ S05 (end): «Kepler's sentence that ran the solar system»
   _Visual: Log-log axes, period vs distance; Mercury to Saturn drop dots; on 'exactly' they snap to a straight line, slope 1.5 (insight sting). Pull-back to the film strip._
